content_metadata.description: Analysis of the political controversy surrounding Tony Abbott's comments about the Australian government and Peter Slipper's resignation as Speaker of the House.

qAndA.question: What logo is visible on the microphone held by Tony Abbott in the video clip?

qAndA.answer: The opposition's motion to remove Mr. Slipper as Speaker, forcing him to make the decision to resign.
qAndA.question: What specific action by the opposition does Paul Fletcher argue led to Mr. Slipper's resignation?

qAndA.answer: The cut to a live feed of the Parliament House.
qAndA.question: What visual element signifies the imminent start of Question Time in Parliament?

qAndA.answer: Findings by a regulator and ongoing police investigations.
qAndA.question: What serious adverse findings of fact does Paul Fletcher say Mr. Thompson has been subject to?

qAndA.answer: Sidebottom argues that it was a deliberate tactic to distract from the real issues. He calls Abbott's comments "insensitive" and "inappropriate."
qAndA.question: What does Sid Sidebottom say about Tony Abbott's use of language regarding the Speaker situation?

activities.description: Newscaster introduces the topic of Tony Abbott's comments about the Australian government.

narrativeProgression.description: Introduction to the topic of Tony Abbott's controversial comments.

activities.description: Tony Abbott defends his use of the phrase 'die of shame' in relation to the Australian government.

narrativeProgression.description: Tony Abbott's explanation of his repeated use of the phrase and why he believes it was not offensive in this context.

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition from the news studio to a video clip of Tony Abbott.

activities.description: Newscaster questions Paul Fletcher about Tony Abbott's justification.
Paul Fletcher discusses the context of the debate regarding the Speaker of the House.
Paul Fletcher criticizes the Labour party for focusing on the language used rather than the Speaker's actions.
Paul Fletcher argues that the opposition's actions led to the Speaker's resignation.
Newscaster questions Sid Sidebottom about the Labour party's actions.
Sid Sidebottom criticizes Tony Abbott's language and calls it a deliberate tactic.
Sid Sidebottom defends the initial appointment of Mr. Slipper as Speaker and his performance in that role.
Paul Fletcher argues against Sid Sidebottom's claims, emphasizing the inappropriateness of Mr. Slipper's actions and language.
Newscaster asks if Sid Sidebottom expects any leadership issues to be ignited and he says Julia Gillard is a fine leader.

characterInteraction.description: Back-and-forth debate between Paul Fletcher and Sid Sidebottom, mediated by the newscaster.

narrativeProgression.description: Panel discussion analyzing Tony Abbott's statement and the surrounding political events.

scenes.title: Panel Debate on Tony Abbott's Comments

videoEditingDetails.description: Transition back to the news studio.
Cut to a live feed of Parliament while the conversation continues.

activities.description: Newscaster thanks guests and wraps up the segment.

climax.description: The debate between Paul Fletcher and Sid Sidebottom regarding the events and the judgment of Julia Gillard.

storylines.description: The controversy surrounding Tony Abbott's comments and the subsequent resignation of Peter Slipper as Speaker of the House.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Welcome back, joining me now in our panel of politicians, the Liberals, Paul Fletcher and Labour's
Sid Side Bottom. Good afternoon to both of you. Before we get started, I do want to play you
another grab from Tony Abbott's door-stop this morning. One of the key criticisms
directed out the opposition leaders to do with his choice of words when he said the government
should die of shame in the Parliament yesterday, Mr Abbott, defended himself this morning.
This phrase has been used by me on at least 17 separate occasions before yesterday,
including in a nationalised address in my televised budget reply. I said that this is a government
that needs to change before it dies of shame. Now, the last thing I want to do is to cause
offence to anyone, but I was absolutely oblivious as I was making that speech to comments that other
people might have made, which were very different and which have been universally condemned,
including by me. Alan Jones said a very insensitive, a very offensive thing,
but it really is time for the Labour Party to stop hyperventilating.
Paul Fletcher, is that really a good enough excuse? Can we really be expected to think that those
Jones comments which dominated the political debate for more than a week had simply
slipped, Mr Abbott's mind yesterday? Well, look, there's been a lot of
emphasis from the Prime Minister and Labour on these kinds of issues, but essentially that missed
the point. Yesterday's debate was about the question of whether the speaker was appropriate
to be in the role and remain in the role, and whether that added to the credibility of the Parliament,
or whether it was time for the speaker to step down. That was the motion that the coalition
moved. That was the context in which Mr Abbott was speaking, and incidentally it was a judgment
which was supposed to be the correct judgment, as we saw in the action, the speaker himself
chose to take correctly later in the day. It was just untenable to have somebody continuing in
that role based upon what we now know about what he's been saying in the whole series of text
messages. So Paul, you're saying that when you heard Mr Abbott say quite a few times yesterday,
this concept of dying of shame in the Parliament, after we've seen so much outrage about those
Jones comments that he didn't cringe even slightly to hear those words coming out of your
leaders mouth. Look, I think there's any connection at all, but clearly it suits the Labour Party to
try and continue to distract from what is the central issue here. The central issue here is whether
it was appropriate that Mr Slipper, Continuous Speaker, in the context of what we now know about
the things that he had said and the attitudes that he had expressed. Clearly it was not appropriate.
The Prime Minister yesterday sought to distract from that issue by focusing on something completely
different in her speech on that motion, but the real question is this, had the opposition not
taken the initiative, would anything have happened? I would, Mr Slipper, still be the speaker,
and I suspect he would, and that would not be to the advantage of the Parliament, and it would not
increase the confidence of the people of Australia in the work of their Parliament.
So, it's our bottom. We haven't seen hypocrisy from Labour here. As Paul Fletcher points out,
everyone on your side today agrees that Mr Slipper did make the right call by resigning,
but when it came to that vote, we saw Labour yesterday trying to protect him. We've seen today,
some of your colleagues saying, well, Parliament isn't a kangaroo court, but if you can't make a decision
on that evidence that no one was disputing when it comes to those text messages, then when
was Labour going to act and make a judgement? Well, I think, first and foremost, the reported
statements of Mr Slipper, are totally inappropriate, and all sides of Parliament have agreed to that,
but let's not forget yesterday was a deliberate tactic of the opposition to use question time
deliberately to raise an issue about the speaker, and for Paul and his colleagues,
and Tony Abbott, to believe that, given that this is a deliberate tactic, that the leader of the
opposition would not have the wherewithal or the forethought to realise what he was saying
was insensitive himself and inappropriate in terms of some of the language he used,
then that reflects very poorly on Mr Abbott and all those that advise him. So he can't just dismiss
this. He knew what he was going to say. It was a deliberate tactic. He knew the language that
he was going to use, and I'm afraid it was hardly insensitive. Now, if he's not aware of that
himself and his colleagues aren't aware of that, then we've got an issue here.
So, it's side of what I would have thought the broader issue is that Labour is now back to square one
with this way for thin majority. It was a mistake to put Mr Slipper in that role initially,
wasn't it in hindsight? Does that decision make some of your colleagues question the Prime Minister's
judgement, let alone her judgement of sticking by him yesterday?
Well, hindsight's mighty thing. I'm sure I could use many, many examples for the leader of the
opposition to contemplate on. Well, allow me to finish that. I'm sure I could use many examples
in terms of hindsight that Mr Abbott could well benefit from. Look, when Mr Slipper was made speaker,
we weren't, and no one was aware of what he was doing privately in terms of his communications.
And, in actual fact, Mr Slipper, I believe, and I was a member of the Speaker's panel for some
time, Mr Slipper did an excellent job in the House as Speaker and conducting himself in terms
of his ceremonial role as well. So, yeah, look, things are easier with hindsight. We can be a lot
more wise in hindsight, but of course, his private communications and what he does with those
communications, how will we to know, how could you know, and indeed, no one he did know?
Well, actually, if I can just respond to that. Paul, I will let you respond to that. I also,
though, Paul, want to, in particular, bring to you to this issue of accepting votes. Isn't
this a ridiculous argument we've heard from the coalition today of where to draw the line,
Mr Abbott saying, well, Craig Thompson's vote is more tainted than Mr Slipper's?
Look, let's start with the question of Julia Gillard's judgment. Julia Gillard showed terrible
judgment yesterday to defend Peter Slipper and focus on trying to keep him as speaker. When,
clearly, it was not appropriate that he remained as Speaker, but there were serious questions raised
about her judgment in November last year when she took the decision to appoint him as Speaker.
This was seen as a masterstroke by some, but there were plenty of people around the Parliament
on both sides of the House who were saying this will come back to bite labour. Only a few months later,
it has. In public life, when you are discharging a job with serious responsibilities, one of the
things you've got to be good at is making judgments about people. I don't think this was a good
judgment that the Prime Minister took and that has been devastated in his days. On this judgment
of accepting votes, Mr Abbott saying that he won't accept Craig Thompson's, he will accept Mr Slipper's.
How does that work? Where exactly does one draw the line here? Well, let's start by making the point
that it's based upon how Mr Slipper has voted since he stepped down. It seems a fairly hypothetical
issue because he's voted with labour, but the key point, the key distinction is that Mr Thompson
has been the subject of serious adverse findings of fact by a regulator and is the subject of ongoing
police investigations. Now, the notion that you should apply the same position to Mr Slipper as
you should to him really is a side show from the central issue, which is, was it appropriate that
Mr Slipper remain a Speaker? Clearly, it wasn't. Was it appropriate for the Prime Minister sort to
defend him in the face of the mounting evidence that was clearly inappropriate in an era of judgment
and it's all been a distraction from the Parliament doing what it is supposed to do, which is
getting on with passing laws and delivering improved outcomes for ordinary Australians.
Well, soon, the Parliament's going to be getting on with question time just quickly before we go there,
live though, said, so I'd bottom up, are you expecting any leadership issues to be ignited from
the drama of the past couple of days? Well, I suspect Tony Abbott will still lead
the coalition, if that's what you mean. Well, exactly what I was suggesting, Sir Edward.
I'm sorry. Oh, right. And let me assure you, Julia Gillard is well and truly in control of
our party and is a fine leader. Make no mistake about it. Okay, it's Sir Edwardham and Paul Fletcher,
we do need to let you run off to question time. Thanks for joining us this afternoon. We do
appreciate it. This afternoon's question.
